claim: The membrane periodic skeleton (MPS) in rat hippocampal neurons is an actomyosin network that controls axonal expansion and contraction.
source: Here, combining chemical and genetic gain- and loss-of-function assays, we show that in rat hippocampal neurons the MPS is an actomyosin network that controls axonal expansion and contraction.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on chemical and genetic assays performed in the study.

claim: Active NMII light chains are colocalized with actin rings and organized in a circular periodic manner throughout the axon shaft.
source: We show that active NMII light chains are colocalized with actin rings and organized in a circular periodic manner throughout the axon shaft.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on super-resolution microscopy analysis.

claim: NMII heavy chains are mostly positioned along the longitudinal axonal axis, being able to crosslink adjacent rings.
source: In contrast, NMII heavy chains are mostly positioned along the longitudinal axonal axis, being able to crosslink adjacent rings.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the positioning of NMII heavy chains based on microscopy data.

claim: NMII filaments can play contractile or scaffolding roles determined by their position relative to actin rings and activation state.
source: NMII filaments can play contractile or scaffolding roles determined by their position relative to actin rings and activation state.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this interpretation of NMII function based on the study's findings.

claim: MPS destabilization through NMII inactivation affects axonal electrophysiology, increasing action potential conduction velocity.
source: We also show that MPS destabilization through NMII inactivation affects axonal electrophysiology, increasing action potential conduction velocity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The mature axon shaft is supported by a submembraneous actin-spectrin network composed of actin rings regularly spaced by spectrin tetramers approximately every 190 nm.
source: The mature axon shaft is supported by a submembraneous actin-spectrin network- the membrane periodic skeleton (MPS)- composed of actin rings regularly spaced by spectrin tetramers approximately every 190 nm (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: The MPS may provide mechanical support for the long thin structure of axons.
source: Although its assembly and function are largely unknown, the MPS may provide mechanical support for the long thin structure of axons (Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hammarlund et al., 2007.

claim: MPS actin rings are made of two long, intertwined actin filaments.
source: Recently, combining platinum-replica electron and optical super-resolution microscopy, the MPS actin rings were shown to be made of two long, intertwined actin filaments (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vassilopoulos et al., 2019.

claim: Adducin is required to maintain axon caliber as its absence in vitro leads to actin rings of increased diameter.
source: We have previously demonstrated that adducin is required to maintain axon caliber as its absence in vitro leads to actin rings of increased diameter, while in vivo it results in progressive axon enlargement and degeneration (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2016, referring to previous work by the authors.

claim: The radius of axonal actin rings narrows over time in vitro.
source: We have additionally found that in vitro, the radius of axonal actin ring narrows over time (Leite et al., 2016), supporting that the MPS has dynamic properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2016.

claim: Reduction in axon diameter with time occurs both in WT and α-adducin knock-out (KO) neurons.
source: Since reduction in axon diameter with time occurs both in WT and α-adducin knock-out (KO) neurons, MPS dynamics is probably regulated by additional actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This observation is stated as a fact leading to an inference about additional regulatory proteins.

claim: The MPS of both WT and α-adducin KO neurons contracts in vitro at a rate of 6–12 nm/day.
source: The MPS of both WT and α-adducin KO neurons contracts in vitro at a rate of 6–12 nm/day (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2016.

claim: Blebbistatin inhibits NMII-mediated ATP hydrolysis and actomyosin-based motility.
source: For that, NMII-mediated ATP hydrolysis and thereby actomyosin-based motility, were inhibited by blebbistatin (Straight et al., 2003; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Straight et al., 2003.

claim: In the presence of blebbistatin, axon thinning of hippocampal neurons from DIV8 to DIV22 was abolished.
source: In the presence of the drug, axon thinning of hippocampal neurons from DIV8 to DIV22 was abolished as determined using Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) microscopy (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C using STED microscopy.

claim: Axon thinning in vitro occurs through a NMII-mediated mechanism.
source: This supports that axon thinning in vitro occurs through a NMII-mediated mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the blebbistatin experiment results.

claim: DIV8 hippocampal neurons treated with blebbistatin had a 1.3-fold increase in axon diameter.
source: Additionally, DIV8 hippocampal neurons treated with blebbistatin had a 1.3-fold increase in axon diameter (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: ML-7 is a selective MLCK inhibitor that decreases pMLC levels in hippocampal neurons.
source: ML-7, a selective MLCK inhibitor that decreases pMLC levels in hippocampal neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), led to an increase in axonal diameter similar to that produced by blebbistatin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: ML-7 led to an increase in axonal diameter similar to that produced by blebbistatin.
source: ML-7, a selective MLCK inhibitor that decreases pMLC levels in hippocampal neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), led to an increase in axonal diameter similar to that produced by blebbistatin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Calyculin A is a potent PP1 inhibitor that results in increased phosphorylation of NMII RLCs and increased myosin contractility.
source: As protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) is the major myosin phosphatase responsible for dephosphorylation of NMII (Matsumura and Hartshorne, 2008), calyculin A, a potent PP1 inhibitor that results in increased phosphorylation of NMII RLCs and increased myosin contractility, was used (Iizuka et al., 1999; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsumura and Hartshorne, 2008 and Iizuka et al., 1999.

claim: In the presence of calyculin A, sustained activation of NMII resulted in a decrease to 0.8-fold in axonal diameter.
source: In the presence of calyculin A, sustained activation of NMII resulted in a decrease to 0.8-fold in axonal diameter (Figure 1D,E), supporting that NMII activity can positively and negatively regulate axonal caliber.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The effect of calyculin A was reverted by blebbistatin.
source: Of note, the effect of calyculin A was reverted by blebbistatin (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Myovin-1 had no effect on the MPS diameter.
source: Myovin-1, a potent inhibitor of the ATPase activity of myosin V that inhibits myosin V-dependent intersynaptic vesicle exchange in hippocampal neurons (Gramlich and Klyachko, 2017), had no effect on the MPS diameter (Figure 1D,E) suggesting a NMII-specific effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E and a citation to Gramlich and Klyachko, 2017.

claim: The effect of blebbistatin was reverted as drug treatment was released from DIV8 to DIV12.
source: In further support of the MPS dynamic nature, the effect of blebbistatin was reverted as drug treatment was released from DIV8 to DIV12 (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Downregulation of either NMIIA or NMIIB induced a 1.3-fold increase in axon caliber.
source: Downregulation of either NMIIA or NMIIB induced a 1.3-fold increase in axon caliber, similar to that induced by either blebbistatin or ML-7 treatment, whereas downregulation of NMIIC was without effect (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: Downregulation of NMIIC was without effect on axon caliber.
source: Downregulation of either NMIIA or NMIIB induced a 1.3-fold increase in axon caliber, similar to that induced by either blebbistatin or ML-7 treatment, whereas downregulation of NMIIC was without effect (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: NMIIC has a distinctive mechanochemical profile and lower ability in generating contractile force when compared with NMIIA and NMIIB isoforms.
source: These results are in agreement with previous studies highlighting the distinctive mechanochemical profile of NMIIC and lower ability in generating contractile force when compared with NMIIA and NMIIB isoforms (Billington et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Billington et al., 2013.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of NMII RLC had a similar effect to the knockdown of myosin heavy chains, leading to MPS expansion.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of NMII RLC (Wang et al., 2008) had a similar effect to the knockdown of myosin heavy chains, leading to MPS expansion (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K and a citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Knocking down MYPT1 caused a decrease to 0.8-fold in axon diameter.
source: Knocking down MYPT1 (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F, K, L) caused a decrease to 0.8-fold in axon diameter (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F, K, L.

claim: Both NMIIA and NMIIB contribute to the MPS actomyosin network.
source: Our data support that both NMIIA and NMIIB, contribute to the MPS actomyosin network.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the knockdown experiments.

claim: No variations in the angle of actin rings in relation to the axonal axis were found after drug- or shRNA-mediated modulation of NMII activity.
source: No variations in the angle of actin rings in relation to the axonal axis were found (Figure 1L,M) suggesting that NMII probably does not contract between adjacent rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L,M.

claim: Neither drug- nor shRNA-mediated modulation of NMII activity resulted in alterations of MPS periodicity.
source: Importantly, neither drug- nor shRNA-mediated modulation of NMII activity, resulted in alterations of MPS periodicity (Figure 1N,O, respectively), thus arguing that a possible participation of NMII in axonal longitudinal tension does not interfere with the 190 nm length of extended spectrin tetramers (Brown et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N,O and a citation to Brown et al., 2015.

claim: Blebbistatin-treated and untreated neurons were electrophysiologically competent regarding signal conduction.
source: Blebbistatin-treated and untreated neurons were electrophysiologically competent regarding signal conduction and no significant differences in global electrical activity were found, as determined by assessing their mean firing rate (MFR) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Axonal conduction velocity between blebbistatin-treated and untreated axons was different, with distinct velocity distributions.
source: However, axonal conduction velocity between treated and untreated axons was different, with distinct velocity distributions (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: From DIV11 on, blebbistatin-treated neurons consistently showed higher propagation velocities when compared to vehicle-treated cells.
source: From DIV11 on, blebbistatin-treated neurons consistently showed higher propagation velocities when compared to vehicle-treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In unmyelinated axons, velocity conduction is proportional to the square root of the axonal diameter.
source: In unmyelinated axons, velocity conduction is proportional to the square root of the axonal diameter (Hodgkin, 1954) and blebbistatin treatment produces a 1.3-fold increase in axon diameter that is not altered throughout time (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hodgkin, 1954.

claim: NMII modulation affects axonal electrophysiology through changes in axonal diameter.
source: Our data favors that NMII modulation affects axonal electrophysiology through changes in axonal diameter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined morphological and electrophysiological data.

claim: pMLC has been described to be specifically localized in the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: pMLC has been described to be specifically localized in the axon initial segment (AIS) (Berger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2018.

claim: Despite the enrichment of pMLC at the AIS, not only non-phosphorylated MLC, but also active pMLC could be observed throughout the entire axon shaft.
source: Despite the enrichment of pMLC at the AIS, not only non-phosphorylated MLC, but also active pMLC could be observed throughout the entire axon shaft (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: pMLC displayed a bilateral ~200 nm periodicity and a circular structure in the AIS.
source: By applying SMLM to the AIS of DIV8 hippocampal neurons and focusing on their lateral outermost points up to the axonal surface, pMLC displayed a bilateral ~200 nm periodicity and a circular structure (Figure 3B,C; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C and Video 1.

claim: Periodic (~190 nm) pMLC staining, coincident with phalloidin staining restricted to the AIS, has been previously shown using STORM.
source: Periodic (~190 nm) pMLC staining, coincident with phalloidin staining restricted to the AIS, has been previously shown using STORM (Berger et al., 2018), suggesting a direct binding of pMLC to actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2018.

claim: pMLC periodicity is not restricted to the AIS, extending to the axon shaft.
source: Here, we show that pMLC periodicity is not restricted to the AIS, extending to the axon shaft, being visible in the lateral outer part of the axon (Figure 3D- highlighted by white ruler; and 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: In some axonal regions, pMLC showed a periodic distribution, consistent with anchoring in different positions of adjacent actin rings.
source: Interestingly, in some axonal regions, pMLC showed a periodic distribution, consistent with anchoring in different positions of adjacent actin rings (Figure 3D- highlighted by red ruler; and Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3F.

claim: In some regions of the axon shaft of hippocampal neurons, pMLC not only displays the expected striped pattern but also is colocalized with actin.
source: However, in some regions of the axon shaft of hippocampal neurons, pMLC not only displays the expected striped pattern but also is colocalized with actin, supporting that throughout the axon, pMLC is bound to actin rings that compose the MPS (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In the axon shaft, pMLC and βII-spectrin intercalate.
source: Simultaneous analysis of βII-spectrin and pMLC using dual color SMLM showed that in the axon shaft the two molecules intercalate (Figure 3H, arrowheads highlight pMLC and asterisks βII-spectrin), whereas a periodic distribution of pMLC consistent with anchoring in different positions of adjacent actin rings also occurs, in both cases non-overlapping with βII spectrin (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Both NMII heavy chain A and NMII heavy chain B were mainly detected within the axon core when focusing the axonal lateral outermost points.
source: When focusing the axonal lateral outermost points, both NMII heavy chain A (Figure 4B) and NMII heavy chain B (Figure 4C) were mainly detected within the axon core.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: At discrete sites, NMIIA and NMIIB colocalized with phalloidin, suggesting that NMII heavy chains might additionally be within individual actin rings.
source: At discrete sites, NMIIA and NMIIB colocalized with phalloidin (Figure 4B,C- highlighted with arrowheads), suggesting that NMII heavy chains might additionally be within individual actin rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: A pattern emerged suggesting the existence of multiple NMIIA heavy chain filaments along the longitudinal axonal axis.
source: When observing axons single-labeled for NMIIA using SMLM, a pattern emerged suggesting the existence of multiple NMIIA heavy chain filaments along the longitudinal axonal axis (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In differentiated SH-SY5Y cells, the approximately 190 nm MPS periodic pattern of βII-spectrin was observed.
source: Of note, in differentiated SH-SY5Y cells, the approximately 190 nm MPS periodic pattern of βII-spectrin was observed (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: In axons of both SH-SY5Y and primary hippocampal neurons, NMIIA can assemble into bipolar filaments of ~300 nm in length.
source: We show that in axons of both cell types, NMIIA can assemble into bipolar filaments of ~300 nm in length, consisting of eGFP puncta at the ends of the filament (N-terminus of head domains) with a single mApple punctum (C-terminus of tail domains) in the middle (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: Fluorescent NMII fusion proteins revealed the existence of multiple consecutive myosin filaments positioned along the axonal axis.
source: Similarly to the data obtained by STORM (Figure 4D), fluorescent NMII fusion proteins revealed the existence of multiple consecutive myosin filaments positioned along the axonal axis (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claim: NMII heavy chain A is mainly positioned within the axon core forming several filaments with different orientations in relation to the axon shaft.
source: Dual color SMLM for the simultaneous analysis of βII-spectrin and NMIIA, further suggested that NMII heavy chain A is mainly positioned within the axon core forming several filaments with different orientations in relation to the axon shaft (Figure 4J; Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and Video 2.

claim: NMIIA filaments are not strictly aligned with the axonal axis.
source: The analysis of the NMIIA labeling envelope, that is, the smooth curve outlining the extremes of NMIIA labeling, showed variable orientations with respect to the axonal longitudinal axis (Figure 4K). This supports that NMIIA filaments are not strictly aligned with the axonal axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: SMLM showed sites of colocalization of NMIIA heavy chain and βII-spectrin, which suggests the existence of NMII filaments crosslinking adjacent rings.
source: SMLM showed sites of colocalization of NMIIA heavy chain and βII-spectrin (Figure 4N), which suggests the existence of NMII filaments crosslinking adjacent rings (Figure 4Q, model a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Immunogold labeling of pMLC followed by platinum-replica electron microscopy showed gold beads along filaments perpendicular to actin rings.
source: Recently, immunogold labeling of pMLC followed by platinum-replica electron microscopy showed gold beads along filaments perpendicular to actin rings (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vassilopoulos et al., 2019.

claim: Some of the NMIIA staining was non-coincident with βII-spectrin, thus pointing towards a possible NMIIA filament distribution within actin rings.
source: One should however note that in our analysis, some of the NMIIA staining was non-coincident with βII-spectrin, thus pointing towards a possible NMIIA filament distribution within actin rings (Figure 4Q, model b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: βII-spectrin showed a prominent peak in the spatial frequency domain, corresponding to a 197 nm periodicity.
source: As expected, βII-spectrin showed a prominent peak in the spatial frequency domain, corresponding to a 197 nm periodicity (Figure 4O, highlighted with #).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: A second pronounced peak at 1.71 µm was observed for βII-spectrin, suggesting a possible secondary structure arrangement of βII-spectrin in axons.
source: Interestingly, a second pronounced peak at 1.71 µm was also observed (Figure 4O, highlighted with *), suggesting a possible secondary structure arrangement of βII-spectrin in axons, that should be the subject of further analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: NMII filaments crosslinking adjacent actin rings are not expected to provide for radial contractility but provide for scaffolding.
source: NMII filaments crosslinking adjacent actin rings (Figure 4P, model a) are not expected to provide for radial contractility but provide for scaffolding.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of NMII filaments based on their position.

claim: NMII filaments within individual actin rings represent the conformation capable of generating the highest contractile force leading to actin filament sliding along the ring.
source: NMII filaments within individual actin rings (Figure 4P, model b), represent the conformation capable of generating the highest contractile force leading to actin filament sliding along the ring.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional role of NMII filaments based on their position.

claim: Assuming that the MPS actin rings are composed of two parallel, intertwined actin filaments, NMII activity could provide for contraction by putting the two actin filaments in registry with each other.
source: Assuming that the MPS actin rings are composed of two parallel, intertwined actin filaments (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019), NMII activity could provide for contraction by putting the two actin filaments in registry with each other.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural model from Vassilopoulos et al., 2019.

claim: In a single ring, NMII filaments with scaffolding and contractile roles might co-exist.
source: It is possible that in a single ring, NMII filaments with scaffolding and contractile roles might co-exist.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about NMII organization.

claim: Scaffolding and contractile roles may switch via change in activity of the NMII motors.
source: Additionally, scaffolding and contractile roles may switch via change in activity of the NMII motors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about NMII function.

claim: The interplay between NMII and deep axonal actin filaments may also occur.
source: One should however bear in mind that despite the fact that NMII activity modulates MPS diameter, and that pMLC colocalizes with MPS actin both in the AIS and in the axon shaft, the interplay between NMII and deep axonal actin filaments may also occur.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative possibilities.

claim: NMII regulates circumferential axonal contraction and expansion.
source: In summary, our data supports that NMII regulates circumferential axonal contraction and expansion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Axon diameter can oscillate depending on organelle transport, neuronal activity, deformations generated by movement or degeneration.
source: When considering an adult axon, its diameter can oscillate depending on organelle transport (Greenberg et al., 1990), neuronal activity (Fields, 2011), deformations generated by movement or degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greenberg et al., 1990 and Fields, 2011.

claim: The mechanisms controlling axonal diameter throughout the neuronal lifetime remain unclear.
source: The mechanisms controlling axonal diameter throughout the neuronal lifetime remain however unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In the initial MPS model, each ring was hypothesized to be composed of actin filaments capped by the actin-binding protein adducin.
source: In the initial MPS model, each ring was hypothesized to be composed of actin filaments capped by the actin-binding protein adducin (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2013.

claim: Adducin might be responsible to enhance the lateral binding of spectrin to actin.
source: According to this novel view, adducin might be responsible to enhance the lateral binding of spectrin to actin.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the novel model of MPS structure.

claim: Absence of adducin in vivo results in progressive axon enlargement and degeneration.
source: We have previously demonstrated that adducin is required to maintain axon caliber as its absence in vitro leads to actin rings of increased diameter, while in vivo it results in progressive axon enlargement and degeneration (Leite et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leite et al., 2016.

claim: MPS dynamics is probably regulated by additional actin-binding proteins.
source: Since reduction in axon diameter with time occurs both in WT and α-adducin knock-out (KO) neurons, MPS dynamics is probably regulated by additional actin-binding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that axon thinning occurs in both WT and adducin KO neurons.

claim: The role of actin in the control of axonal radial tension is emerging.
source: The role of actin in the control of axonal radial tension is emerging (Costa et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2018 and Fan et al., 2017.

claim: NMII is a hexamer composed by two heavy chains, two regulatory light chains (RLC) and two essential light chains (ELC).
source: NMII is a hexamer composed by two heavy chains, two regulatory light chains (RLC) and two essential light chains (ELC), being a conserved molecule for generating mechanical forces (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: The NMII contractile ATPase activity and the assembly of myosin filaments that coordinate force generation is activated by phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC).
source: The NMII contractile ATPase activity and the assembly of myosin filaments that coordinate force generation is activated by phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: The axonal MPS is an actomyosin-II network that regulates circumferential axonal contractility.
source: Here, we provide evidence that the axonal MPS, similarly to actin rings present in other biological contexts, is an actomyosin-II network that regulates circumferential axonal contractility.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: The MPS affects signal propagation velocity.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MPS affects signal propagation velocity, a property with important functional implications.
evidence: This is a summary statement of a key finding of the study.

claim: Inhibiting both adducin levels and NMII activity did not result in a cumulative effect on axonal caliber.
source: Whereas inhibiting NMII activity or knocking down adducin led to a 1.3-fold increase in axonal caliber, being the latter case in agreement with our previous studies in adducin KO neurons (Leite et al., 2016), the combination of both treatments did not result in a cumulative effect (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H,I and a citation to Leite et al., 2016.

claim: Different NMII isoforms have unique kinetic properties and specific cellular functions.
source: Different NMII isoforms have unique kinetic properties and specific cellular functions (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: Knockdown of either NMIIA or NMIIB was sufficient to induce a comparable outcome as drug-mediated inhibition of all NMII isoforms.
source: As such, knockdown of either NMIIA or NMIIB was sufficient to induce a comparable outcome as drug-mediated inhibition of all NMII isoforms, whereas NMIIC probably does not participate in NMII-mediated regulation of axon diameter.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of knockdown and drug treatment experiments.

claim: MYPT1 is the regulatory subunit of myosin light chain phosphatase and is responsible for the dephosphorylation of MLC.
source: Myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1) is the regulatory subunit of myosin light chain phosphatase and is responsible for the dephosphorylation of MLC.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about MYPT1 function.

claim: The inactivation of MYPT1 enzymatic activity increases NMII phosphorylation and consequently its activation.
source: The inactivation of its enzymatic activity increases NMII phosphorylation and consequently its activation (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: Rescue experiments performed using co-transfection with shRNA-resistant constructs reverted the phenotype of the corresponding shRNA, confirming their specificity.
source: Of note, rescue experiments performed using co-transfection with shRNA-resistant constructs reverted the phenotype of the corresponding shRNA, confirming their specificity (Figure 1J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,K.

claim: Tilting may be hindered by the existence of the βII-spectrin scaffold.
source: Of note, tilting may be hindered by the existence of the βII-spectrin scaffold.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about why tilting was not observed.

claim: Having several active NMII filaments attached to adjacent axon rings may generate a net force that would be averaged out and thus close to zero.
source: Also, having several active NMII filaments attached to adjacent axon rings, may generate a net force that would be averaged out and thus close to zero.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about force distribution in the MPS.

claim: A possible participation of NMII in axonal longitudinal tension does not interfere with the 190 nm length of extended spectrin tetramers.
source: Importantly, neither drug- nor shRNA-mediated modulation of NMII activity, resulted in alterations of MPS periodicity (Figure 1N,O, respectively), thus arguing that a possible participation of NMII in axonal longitudinal tension does not interfere with the 190 nm length of extended spectrin tetramers (Brown et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that MPS periodicity was not altered, supported by a citation to Brown et al., 2015.

claim: Neuronal electrophysiology is intimately related to morphology.
source: Neuronal electrophysiology is intimately related to morphology.
evidence: This is a statement of general knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Sodium channels are distributed in axons in a periodic pattern coordinated with the MPS.
source: Besides the relation between conduction velocity and axonal caliber (Hodgkin, 1954; Waxman, 1980), sodium channels are distributed in axons in a periodic pattern coordinated with the MPS (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hodgkin, 1954; Waxman, 1980; and Xu et al., 2013.

claim: The μEF platform allows axon alignment on top of a sequence of microelectrodes, providing detailed electrophysiological information about signal conduction on isolated axons.
source: This μEF platform was previously shown by us to allow axon alignment on top of a sequence of microelectrodes, providing detailed electrophysiological information about signal conduction on isolated axons (Figure 2A) while also recording global activity levels (Heiney et al., 2019; Lopes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heiney et al., 2019 and Lopes et al., 2018.

claim: No significant differences in global electrical activity were found between blebbistatin-treated and untreated neurons.
source: Blebbistatin-treated and untreated neurons were electrophysiologically competent regarding signal conduction and no significant differences in global electrical activity were found, as determined by assessing their mean firing rate (MFR) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment produces a 1.3-fold increase in axon diameter that is not altered throughout time.
source: In unmyelinated axons, velocity conduction is proportional to the square root of the axonal diameter (Hodgkin, 1954) and blebbistatin treatment produces a 1.3-fold increase in axon diameter that is not altered throughout time (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and a citation to Hodgkin, 1954.

claim: pMLC regulates the head groups of the NMII heavy chains, mediating their binding to actin and the organization of NMII into bipolar filaments.
source: pMLC regulates the head groups of the NMII heavy chains, mediating their binding to actin and the organization of NMII into bipolar filaments (Berger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2018.

claim: In each actin ring a limited number of pMLC molecules is anchored.
source: The absence of a generalized striped pattern for pMLC (in contrast to what is observed for axonal actin and βII-spectrin staining), supports that in each actin ring a limited number of pMLC molecules is anchored.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed staining pattern.

claim: Technical limitations of the antibodies used may preclude the visualization of the entire pool of pMLC molecules present in the structure.
source: Alternatively, technical limitations of the antibodies used may preclude the visualization of the entire pool of pMLC molecules present in the structure.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential technical limitations.

claim: Throughout the axon, pMLC is bound to actin rings that compose the MPS.
source: However, in some regions of the axon shaft of hippocampal neurons, pMLC not only displays the expected striped pattern but also is colocalized with actin, supporting that throughout the axon, pMLC is bound to actin rings that compose the MPS (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A periodic distribution of pMLC consistent with anchoring in different positions of adjacent actin rings occurs, non-overlapping with βII spectrin.
source: Simultaneous analysis of βII-spectrin and pMLC using dual color SMLM showed that in the axon shaft the two molecules intercalate (Figure 3H, arrowheads highlight pMLC and asterisks βII-spectrin), whereas a periodic distribution of pMLC consistent with anchoring in different positions of adjacent actin rings also occurs, in both cases non-overlapping with βII spectrin (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The localization of NMIIA and NMIIB within axons did not differ significantly.
source: Although no simultaneous labeling of NMIIA and NMIIB was performed given host antibody constraints, their localization within axons did not differ significantly (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The organization of NMIIA clearly contrasted with the circular periodic distribution of pMLC.
source: Of note, this organization clearly contrasted with the circular periodic distribution of pMLC (Figure 3B; Video 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between the observed distributions of NMIIA and pMLC.

claim: The analysis of the NMIIA labeling envelope showed variable orientations with respect to the axonal longitudinal axis.
source: The analysis of the NMIIA labeling envelope, that is, the smooth curve outlining the extremes of NMIIA labeling, showed variable orientations with respect to the axonal longitudinal axis (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: These filaments might correspond to myosins associated with the MPS, cross-linking neighboring rings.
source: This led to the hypothesis that these filaments might correspond to myosins associated with the MPS, cross-linking neighboring rings, which goes along our observations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Vassilopoulos et al., 2019 that is consistent with the current observations.

claim: A possible secondary structure arrangement of βII-spectrin in axons should be the subject of further analysis.
source: Interestingly, a second pronounced peak at 1.71 µm was also observed (Figure 4O, highlighted with *), suggesting a possible secondary structure arrangement of βII-spectrin in axons, that should be the subject of further analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions based on the observed data.

claim: When axonal diameter is restored, contractile NMII filaments may perform ring contraction, favored by transient absence of scaffolding filaments.
source: When axonal diameter is restored, contractile NMII filaments may perform ring contraction, favored by transient absence of scaffolding filaments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the dynamics of NMII function.

claim: Eventually, scaffolding NMII may be restored and contraction may slow down to its original low rate.
source: Eventually, scaffolding NMII may be restored and contraction may slow down to its original low rate.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the dynamics of NMII function.

claim: In physiological responses at an initial stage, scaffolding NMII may be reduced to a minimum, while contractile filaments cannot prevent ring expansion.
source: In physiological responses (such as axon diameter increase upon cargo trafficking) at an initial stage, scaffolding NMII may be reduced to a minimum, while contractile filaments cannot prevent ring expansion.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about physiological mechanisms.

claim: At a second stage (when cargo moves), contractile NMII may lead to a fast return to the original diameter.
source: At a second stage (when cargo moves), contractile NMII may lead to a fast return to the original diameter.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about physiological mechanisms.

claim: Eventually, scaffolding filaments may be restored and the contraction rate will return to a very low value.
source: Eventually, scaffolding filaments may be restored and the contraction rate will return to a very low value.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about physiological mechanisms.

claim: The possibility that alternative axonal actin arrangements may also serve as myosin anchors cannot be ruled out.
source: In this scenario, the possibility that these alternative axonal actin arrangements may also serve as myosin anchors cannot be ruled out and should be certainly explored in the future.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative possibilities for future research.

claim: These findings have important implications on our understanding of neuronal biology, including fluctuations in axonal diameter observed during trafficking, action potential firing and axon degeneration.
source: These findings have important implications on our understanding of neuronal biology, including fluctuations in axonal diameter observed during trafficking, action potential firing and axon degeneration.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of the study's findings.

claim: PP1 is the major myosin phosphatase responsible for dephosphorylation of NMII.
source: As protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) is the major myosin phosphatase responsible for dephosphorylation of NMII (Matsumura and Hartshorne, 2008), calyculin A, a potent PP1 inhibitor that results in increased phosphorylation of NMII RLCs and increased myosin contractility, was used (Iizuka et al., 1999; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsumura and Hartshorne, 2008.

claim: MLCK phosphorylates the NMII RLCs leading to conformational changes and self-assembly in myosin filaments.
source: The function of NMII is controlled by MLC kinase (MLCK) that phosphorylates the NMII RLCs leading to conformational changes and self-assembly in myosin filaments (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009.

claim: Pharmacological NMII inhibition may lead to ring expansion given loss of both scaffolding and contractile roles.
source: Pharmacological NMII inhibition may lead to ring expansion given loss of both scaffolding and contractile roles; as a consequence, the inner axonal tension will lead to increased axon diameter.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed effects.

claim: A non-uniform distribution of NMII along the actin structures cannot generate significant contractile force but rather hold a crosslinking function.
source: One should however note that from the images presented (Vassilopoulos et al., 2019), a non-uniform distribution of NMII along the actin structures is observed which, to our understanding, cannot generate significant contractile force but rather hold a crosslinking function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from images in Vassilopoulos et al., 2019.
